evidence.snippet: We identified four specific, dominantly acting SPTLC1 variants in seven families manifesting as childhood-onset ALS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes dominant (heterozygous) action of the ALS-causing SPTLC1 variants.

evidence.snippet: all patients in this family carried the same SPTLC1 variant (NM_006415.4:c.115_117delCTT, p.(L39del)), which was recurrent in two unrelated childhood ALS patients
evidence.explanation: Documents the recurrent p.Leu39del allele and its transmission within a pedigree.

steps/1.description: Dominant SPTLC1 variants associated with ALS include transmembrane-region missense and short deletions, as well as a splice-altering c.58G>T allele. Biochemical effects are allele-specific. S331 substitutions near the catalytic region can produce overlapping sensory-autonomic and motor disease and should not be treated as transmembrane-cluster alleles.

evidence.snippet: Rather than the predicted amino acid substitution p.(A20S), this variant predominantly resulted in complete skipping of exon 2, which is predicted to result in in-frame deletion of amino acids 20–56 comprising the entire first transmembrane domain of the SPTLC1 protein18.
evidence.explanation: Primary non-neural transcript result.

evidence.snippet: No band corresponding to exon 2 skipping (266 bp) was detected
evidence.explanation: Negative lymphoblast RT-PCR result for c.58G>A, not proof about every tissue.

steps/2.description: The c.58G>T allele predominantly skips exon 2 and deletes the transmembrane domain in sampled blood/cultured cells. In contrast, c.58G>A retained exon 2 in one patient lymphoblast line. Neural-tissue splicing was not measured, and the two nucleotide changes should not be assigned the same mechanism.

evidence.snippet: We show that ORMDL binding to the holoenzyme complex is impaired in cells expressing pathogenic SPTLC1-ALS alleles, resulting in increased SL synthesis and a distinct lipid signature.
evidence.explanation: Co-immunoprecipitation and native-complex experiments, with variant and system limits.

steps/3.description: Reduced association with ORMDL regulatory proteins was measured for several variants in engineered cells and for selected patient fibroblast preparations. Y23F retained association in the 2022 study; C133W also showed reduced association without the same canonical-lipid feedback defect. Purified ALS-variant complexes in the 2023 study retained ORMDL. Thus association loss is one possible route to dysregulation, not a necessary or sufficient explanation for every allele.

evidence.snippet: Our results, in which ORMDL3 is apparently associated with the complexes containing the SPTLC1 variants, demonstrate that the unrestrained sphingolipid biosynthesis caused by SPTLC1 ALS variants is associated, at least in part, with impaired ceramide sensing of these variants when ORMDL is contained within the SPT complex.
evidence.explanation: Primary biochemical findings; the Y23A/Y23F discrepancy prevents equating all tested constructs with patient alleles.

steps/4.description: Recombinant human SPT-ORMDL complexes containing selected ALS-associated variants were less inhibited by short-chain ceramide despite ORMDL retention. Structural and engineered-mutant experiments support a ceramide-sensing site; the precise allosteric effect of each patient allele was not structurally resolved. Short-chain substrate assays and detergent-purified complexes do not reproduce all native membrane conditions.

evidence.snippet: These variants disrupt the normal homeostatic regulation of serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) by ORMDL proteins, resulting in unregulated SPT activity and elevated levels of canonical SPT products.
evidence.explanation: Primary cellular activity and lipid synthesis experiments.

steps/5.description: SPT normally undergoes homeostatic regulation by ORMDL proteins and ceramide. Several ALS-associated variants blunt that inhibition while retaining catalytic activity. The degree and route of escape depend on the allele and experimental system.

evidence.snippet: Canonical sphingolipids ceramides and glucosyl ceramides (glucCer) are increased in p.F40_S41del iPSC-hMNs compared to their isogenic control and increase further in the double mutant iPSC-hMNs.
evidence.explanation: Stable-isotope labeling of engineered WTC11-derived cells; monoallelic and compound lines were both studied.

steps/6.description: Isotope-labeling experiments show increased formation of canonical sphingolipids in selected patient fibroblasts and engineered cells, including monoallelic F40_S41del motor neuron-like cells. This is distinct from a steady-state concentration assay and is not established for every tissue or allele.

evidence.snippet: Particularily dihydro-sphingolipids (dhSL) were signficantly increased in patient plasma and p.L38R mutant expressing cells.
evidence.explanation: Identifies dihydrosphingolipids as the most raised species in patient plasma (quoted verbatim, including the source's typographical errors).

evidence.snippet: The levels of complex ceramides, including lactosylceramide, hexosylceramide, and sphingomyelin, did not significantly differ across family members.
evidence.explanation: Negative lipid-class result limits any assertion of globally increased lipids.

steps/7.description: Selected patient plasma and cell samples show elevated canonical sphingoid bases, dihydrosphingolipids or ceramides. Species and lipid classes differ across individuals and experiments; not all complex lipids rise. A later family study compared one proband with two parents using repeated measurements, not independent patient replicates. The lipid-to-neuronal-injury bridge remains inferred.

evidence.snippet: All six individuals had upper and lower motor neuron signs and symptoms in the cranial, cervical and lumbar myotomes and thus met the revised El Escorial criteria for the clinical definition of ALS
evidence.explanation: Clinical upper and lower motor neuron findings in six selected probands.

steps/8.description: Spasticity, hyperreflexia and pyramidal signs establish upper motor neuron involvement in many reported patients. These signs can be absent in individual cases, and upper motor neuron dysfunction need not precede weakness. Human clinical signs do not provide direct counts of cortical neuron loss.

evidence.snippet: All six individuals had upper and lower motor neuron signs and symptoms in the cranial, cervical and lumbar myotomes and thus met the revised El Escorial criteria for the clinical definition of ALS
evidence.explanation: Clinical localization, rather than autopsy neuron counts.

steps/9.description: Clinical weakness, atrophy, fasciculations and multi-myotomal denervation support lower motor neuron disease. Sensory findings were normal in many transmembrane-variant cases, but mixed SPTLC1 phenotypes and intrafamilial variation prevent an absolute motor-only rule.

evidence.snippet: Four patients had undergone a muscle biopsy, which demonstrated acute and chronic neurogenic changes
evidence.explanation: Four diagnostic biopsies showed neurogenic change.

steps/10.description: Denervated muscle shows neurogenic atrophy and acute or chronic electrodiagnostic changes. Limb, bulbar and respiratory muscle involvement produces variable disability; respiratory failure can develop while the patient is still ambulant. Mild inflammation in one muscle specimen does not establish a primary inflammatory myopathy or a causal inflammatory pathway.

evidence.snippet: We identified six individuals from six unrelated families who developed early-childhood-onset lower extremity spasticity manifesting as toe walking and gait abnormalities followed by progressive lower motor neuron-mediated weakness without sensory symptoms or signs
evidence.explanation: Clinical presentation of six selected index probands; this does not establish a disease-wide frequency.

steps/11.description: Lower-limb spasticity and toe walking were presenting findings in the six original unrelated probands, but some later patients presented predominantly with weakness or lacked classic pyramidal signs. No population frequency is inferred from selected cases.

evidence.snippet: followed by progressive lower motor neuron-mediated weakness without sensory symptoms or signs
evidence.explanation: Progressive lower motor neuron weakness in all six index-cohort probands.

evidence.snippet: The patient presented with muscular weakness and atrophy, tongue tremor and fasciculation, breathing problems and positive pyramidal signs.
evidence.explanation: Independent case confirming the weakness/atrophy phenotype.

steps/12.description: Progressive weakness affects limb and sometimes bulbar or respiratory muscles. Proximal, distal and asymmetric presentations occur; lower motor neuron weakness does not invariably follow a prior spastic phase.

evidence.snippet: Her neurological examination at presentation revealed a body mass index less than the first percentile, exaggerated lumbar lordosis, tongue fasciculations and wasting, generalized muscle atrophy and weakness, brisk asymmetric ankle reflexes, a positive Gower sign, and normal sensation
evidence.explanation: Documents generalized muscle atrophy and weakness with preserved sensation in an ALS27 patient.

steps/13.description: Generalized or regionally predominant neurogenic muscle wasting accompanies weakness. Proximal weakness can produce a Gowers sign or lordosis.

evidence.snippet: this initial manifestation was almost universally followed by diffuse and progressive lower motor neuron degeneration, including tongue fasciculations, which is highly unusual for classic forms of HSP but consistent with ALS
evidence.explanation: The source describes progressive lower motor neuron involvement including tongue fasciculations; the wording does not provide a separate tongue-fasciculation numerator.

steps/14.description: Tongue fasciculations are a reported bulbar lower motor neuron sign and can distinguish ALS from a classic pure spastic-paraplegia presentation; they are not documented in every case.

evidence.snippet: She experienced gradual decline in muscle strength with development of weakness and hyperreflexia in lower extremities and diffuse fasciculations in the upper extremities at 26 years.
evidence.explanation: The longitudinal L39del patient developed hyperreflexia; this avoids relying solely on the mixed S331Y case.

steps/15.description: Brisk or exaggerated deep tendon reflexes, including an exaggerated jaw jerk, reflect the upper motor neuron component of ALS27.

evidence.snippet: She experienced gradual decline in muscle strength with development of weakness and hyperreflexia in lower extremities and diffuse fasciculations in the upper extremities at 26 years.
evidence.explanation: Documents diffuse fasciculations alongside weakness and hyperreflexia in a genetically confirmed ALS27 patient.

steps/16.description: Diffuse fasciculations in limb and bulbar muscles are a lower motor neuron sign in ALS27.

evidence.snippet: De novo variants in SPTLC1 (p.Ala20Ser in 2 patients and p.Ser331Tyr in 1 patient) were identified in 3 unrelated patients diagnosed with juvenile ALS and failure to thrive.
evidence.explanation: Three of the four probands in this study carried a juvenile ALS diagnosis together with failure to thrive.

evidence.snippet: Patient 1 presented with gradually progressive spastic diplegia and growth retardation beginning at age 5 years.
evidence.explanation: Growth retardation from early childhood in an ALS27 patient.

steps/17.description: Poor weight gain or low body mass was prominent in a growth-ascertained juvenile case series, including a mixed S331Y phenotype. Other patients had normal weight. Selected enrollment and incomplete assessment preclude a population frequency.

evidence.snippet: The disease was universally progressive and led to loss of independent ambulation and respiratory insufficiency of variable degrees.
evidence.explanation: Respiratory involvement in the original selected series, with variable severity and timing.

genes/0.notes: SPTLC1 encodes an SPT subunit. Heterozygous transmembrane-region variants include Y23F, L38R, L39del and F40_S41del. c.58G>T predominantly alters splicing, whereas c.58G>A retained exon 2 in one non-neural assay despite sharing codon 20. Sequence, transcript and protein-level interpretations must be distinguished. The p.Leu38Arg case-report title has discordant nucleotide/protein notation, so only the protein designation is used here. S331 substitutions can produce mixed sensory-autonomic and motor disease. Neither variant position alone nor a single plasma lipid result determines clinical classification.

treatments/14.description: One compassionate-use patient gained weight without demonstrated neurological improvement. A HEK293FT study reported substrate-preference and mitochondrial-probe changes improved by serine, whereas isotope-labeled motor neuron-like cells showed increased canonical lipid production with serine availability. The substrate-preference result was not reproduced under another study's conditions. These are different assays and alleles; neither clinical benefit nor clinical worsening is established. Supplementation is not an established ALS27 treatment, and a theoretical risk of increasing lipid production warrants specialist caution.

evidence.snippet: We do not yet understand why motor and sensory neurons show selective vulnerability to distinct biochemical changes in sphingolipid synthesis and homeostasis.
evidence.explanation: Explicit unresolved mechanism.

open_questions/0.rationale: Human genetics and cell experiments establish altered regulation and synthesis, but the selective neuronal injury pathway remains unresolved. Plasma concentrations do not localize the relevant tissue exposure. Candidate mitochondrial and inflammatory signals in non-neural cells do not establish necessary mediators. Sensory-motor overlap also argues against a strict two-disease dichotomy.

evidence.snippet: It remains unclear whether sufficient ΔE2 protein is available in vivo to incorporate into the SPT complex or interact with ORMDL proteins.
evidence.explanation: The key unmeasured molecular parameter.

evidence.snippet: Using CRISPR, we created one iPSC line heterozygous for p.(F40_S41del), akin to patient 3 and another line compound heterozygous for p.(F40_S41del) and a deletion of exon 2 (the consequence of the c.58 G > T variant), which would be predicted to further exacerbate the biochemical phenotype.
evidence.explanation: Both monoallelic and compound engineered lines were studied.

open_questions/1.rationale: The deletion models a real human splice consequence, so mismatch cannot be dismissed as an unrelated lesion. Homozygous lethality does not establish simple enzymatic loss of function. The mutant protein, complex incorporation and flux were not directly resolved. Human-cell evidence includes both monoallelic and compound engineered motor neuron-like cells; criticism of the compound line does not erase the monoallelic result.

evidence.snippet: We did not observe evidence of neurological improvement, although prolonged therapy would be required to detect such an effect.
evidence.explanation: Clinical observation without control.

evidence.snippet: Limiting L-serine availability in SPTLC1-ALS-expressing cells increased 1-deoxySL and shifted the SL profile from an ALS to an HSAN1-like signature.
evidence.explanation: Experimental countervailing concern for substrate restriction.

open_questions/2.rationale: A HEK293FT assay and one compassionate-use case suggest possible biochemical or weight effects, while engineered neuronal lipid assays and mechanistic reviews raise concern about increasing canonical lipid production. Clinical neurological benefit and harm remain unproven. Serine restriction is also not an established therapy: low-serine cultures can increase deoxysphingolipids. The low-serine L39del carrier provides an association, not proof of diet-induced phenotype conversion.

evidence.snippet: Further investigations are necessary to determine whether there is a threshold for the relative abundance of mutant alleles in the clinical presentation of ALS.
evidence.explanation: Authors explicitly leave the threshold unresolved.

open_questions/3.rationale: One clinically unaffected parent had 17% blood mosaicism, but brain and germline fractions were unmeasured and lipid levels were not a consistent intermediate phenotype. This does not define a safe threshold or predict the amount of therapeutic knockdown needed.

steps/3.description: An experimentally supported contributor to trisomy 21-associated cardiac development. evidence.snippet: In each case the p.R329C mutation was inherited from an unaffected parent.
evidence.explanation: Human penetrance limit for this susceptibility allele.

evidence.snippet: Our study identifies the Cysteine-Rich with EGF-Like Domains 1 (Creld1) gene as a regulator of calcineurin/NFATc1 signaling.
evidence.explanation: Experimental mechanism from the available primary abstract.

steps/4.description: CRELD1 susceptibility variants and murine loss-of-function experiments support a contribution to cardiac development. Heterozygous variants can be inherited from unaffected people; complete mouse knockout is not equivalent to every human allele.

evidence.snippet: Creld1 is contained in a joint protein complex with the regulatory subunit of calcineurin, CnB, thereby controlling calcineurin function.
evidence.explanation: Primary mechanistic abstract; detailed full-text assays were not retrievable.

evidence.snippet: We show that Creld1 is sufficient to promote NFATc1 dephosphorylation and translocation to the nucleus.
evidence.explanation: Dephosphorylation and localization are separated into distinct events.

steps/5.description: The proposed molecular lesion is reduced activation of NFATC1 through dephosphorylation. ER-localized CRELD1 participates in a complex with calcineurin B. VEGF is an upstream stimulus in the developmental experiments, not an established downstream product of CRELD1.

evidence.explanation: HepG2 APOB repression is preserved despite variant-specific activation changes in HEK293T cells.

evidence.snippet: reduction of HMGN1 to two copies in trisomic cells partially restored the transcriptional dysregulation to a more disomic-like state
evidence.explanation: Primary correction result in human cultured cardiomyocytes.

evidence.snippet: After stimulation with ionomycin, a large fraction of the p.(Ala367Val) and p.(Ala696Thr) NFATC1 proteins was retained in the cytoplasm

evidence.explanation: Clinical morphogenesis summary, complemented by the broader developmental review.

evidence.snippet: In complete AVSDs, there is typically a large left-to-right shunt in early infancy.
evidence.explanation: Complete-form clinical physiology.

steps/18.description: Atrial and, where present, ventricular communications permit excess left-to-right flow after pulmonary vascular resistance falls. Flow magnitude differs between complete, restrictive transitional and partial defects and can change with pulmonary vascular disease.

evidence.snippet: The large left-to-right shunt causes excessive blood flow to the lungs, resulting in increased pulmonary artery pressures.
evidence.explanation: Flow/pressure sequence described in clinical review.

steps/19.description: Increased pulmonary flow is a hemodynamic consequence of substantial shunting; it contributes to respiratory symptoms and pressure load. It is distinct from fixed pulmonary vascular remodeling.

evidence.snippet: CHF results from significant communication between the atria and ventricles, leading to volume overload in both the right atrium and the right ventricle.
evidence.explanation: Clinical physiology.

steps/20.description: Excess shunt flow and valve regurgitation place volume demands on the circulation. The affected chamber pattern depends on the specific anatomy and valve lesion.

evidence.snippet: CHF symptoms are primarily secondary to pulmonary overcirculation
evidence.explanation: Clinical hemodynamic rather than intrinsic cardiomyopathy framing.

steps/21.description: Symptomatic heart failure reflects inability to accommodate the hemodynamic burden, particularly in infancy with significant shunting. It is not necessarily a primary myocardial contractile disease.

evidence.snippet: Those who survive beyond 1 year develop irreversible pulmonary vascular disease, and later on, the reversal of the shunt.
evidence.explanation: Historical clinical synthesis; the universal wording is not adopted across all AVSD subtypes.

evidence.snippet: demonstrating Eisenmenger physiology or ... >10 Wood units, shunt closure should ... not ... be performed to avoid additional morbidity and mortality.

evidence.snippet: The aberrant expression of recoverin in cancer cells and the presence of autoantibodies against recoverin are essential for the occurrence of cancer-associated retinopathy, which finally results in the apoptosis of photoreceptor cells.

evidence.snippet: Cancer-associated retinal ON bipolar cell dysfunction (CARBD), which includes melanoma-associated retinopathy (MAR), has been reported to be caused by autoantibodies against the molecules expressed in ON bipolar cells, including TRPM1.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates TRPM1 as the primary target antigen in MAR-related ON bipolar cell dysfunction, confirming the molecular mimicry mechanism for the MAR subtype.

steps/0.description: In CAR, tumor cells aberrantly express retinal proteins (most prominently recoverin/ RCVRN) or proteins sharing epitopes with retinal antigens, and the resulting immune response drives B-cell production of anti-retinal IgG autoantibodies (molecular mimicry). The exact mechanisms by which ocular immune privilege breaks down and self-tolerance is lost remain unknown. In MAR, melanoma cells express TRPM1 (transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 1), which is also expressed in retinal ON-bipolar cells; the resulting anti-TRPM1 antibodies disrupt bipolar-cell signaling. In nonparaneoplastic AIR (npAIR), the inciting trigger is unknown but similar anti-retinal autoantibodies arise without detectable malignancy, possibly in association with concurrent systemic autoimmune disease.

evidence.snippet: The aberrant expression of recoverin in cancer cells and the presence of autoantibodies against recoverin are essential for the occurrence of cancer-associated retinopathy, which finally results in the apoptosis of photoreceptor cells.
evidence.explanation: Links anti-recoverin autoantibody activity in CAR to photoreceptor apoptosis, the cell injury asserted by this node.

evidence.snippet: AIRs are a group of inflammatory conditions affecting the retina characterized by progressive unexplained visual loss, abnormalities and contraction in visual fields, photoreceptor and electroretinographic dysfunction, and the presence of circulating anti-retinal antibodies.
evidence.explanation: Links circulating anti-retinal antibodies to photoreceptor dysfunction and electroretinographic abnormalities, supporting antibody-mediated retinal injury.

evidence.snippet: Structural changes at the baseline were detected in 14 of 16 (87.5%) eyes on WAFP and WAFAF and 13 of 16 (81.2%) eyes on SD-OCT.
evidence.explanation: Longitudinal cohort data quantifying high rates of structural retinal injury in npAIR using multimodal imaging, consistent with progressive autoantibody-mediated photoreceptor destruction.

steps/1.description: Anti-retinal autoantibodies penetrate the outer retina and cause cell-type-specific injury. In CAR, anti-recoverin antibodies target recoverin, the calcium-binding protein that normally controls rhodopsin phosphorylation by inhibiting rhodopsin kinase, and their presence culminates in photoreceptor apoptosis. Anti-alpha-enolase antibodies are also among the most commonly detected autoantibodies in CAR. In MAR, anti-TRPM1 antibodies enter ON-bipolar cells and block TRPM1 channel function, producing a characteristic electronegative ERG. The result is progressive, largely irreversible photoreceptor and inner retinal neuronal loss that clinically mimics inherited retinal dystrophies.

evidence.snippet: AIRs are a group of inflammatory conditions affecting the retina characterized by progressive unexplained visual loss, abnormalities and contraction in visual fields, photoreceptor and electroretinographic dysfunction, and the presence of circulating anti-retinal antibodies.
evidence.explanation: Identifies progressive visual field contraction as a defining clinical feature of the entire AIR spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Visual impairment was bilateral in over 90% of cases.
evidence.explanation: Systematic review of 147 paraneoplastic ocular syndrome patients (including 53 CAR and 22 MAR) reports bilateral visual impairment in over 90% of the pooled cases across all six syndromes reviewed.

steps/2.description: Progressive constriction of visual fields with ring scotomas or diffuse loss, developing over weeks to months. In CAR, loss is typically rapid and bilateral; in MAR, central vision may be relatively preserved with more prominent nyctalopia and peripheral field defects. A systematic review of paraneoplastic ocular syndromes found visual impairment to be bilateral in over 90% of cases.

evidence.explanation: Reduced night vision is enumerated among the defining visual deficits of MAR, directly supporting nyctalopia as an AIR phenotype.

evidence.snippet: An 84-year-old female presented with bilateral scotomas and progressive nyctalopia over 1 year.
evidence.explanation: CAR case report documenting progressive nyctalopia as a presenting symptom.

evidence.explanation: Rod ERG dysfunction is an electrophysiological correlate consistent with night blindness, but this case series does not report nyctalopia as a symptom, so the inference to the clinical phenotype is indirect.

steps/3.description: Night blindness is a prominent early feature, particularly in MAR where anti-TRPM1 antibodies target ON-bipolar cells and impair scotopic signal processing, and in CAR where rod photoreceptors are preferentially affected initially.

evidence.snippet: patients develop vision deficits that include reduced night vision, poor contrast sensitivity, and photopsia

steps/4.description: Flickering, shimmering, or flashing lights (photopsias) are a characteristic early symptom, especially in MAR where anti-TRPM1 antibodies block ON-bipolar cell signaling. Photopsias may also arise from ectopic photoreceptor excitation in CAR.

evidence.snippet: The aberrant expression of recoverin in cancer cells and the presence of autoantibodies against recoverin are essential for the occurrence of cancer-associated retinopathy, which finally results in the apoptosis of photoreceptor cells.

evidence.snippet: The visual symptoms arise when TRPM1 autoantibodies enter ON-BCs and block the function of TRPM1, thus detection of TRPM1 autoantibodies in patient serum is a key criterion in diagnosing MAR.
evidence.explanation: States the antibody-to-cell-injury step explicitly for the MAR arm: circulating autoantibody must reach and enter the target retinal neuron to produce dysfunction. The same report finds intraocular corticosteroid relieves symptoms despite persistently high circulating antibody, which is why antibody access across the blood-retinal barrier, not titre alone, is modeled as the causal step.

evidence.snippet: The spectrum includes primary autoimmune diseases and associations with retinitis pigmentosa or various malignancies, raising questions about the causative role of antibodies.
evidence.explanation: Cuts against this edge rather than supporting it. The 2025 review records that the pathogenicity of anti-retinal antibodies (anti-recoverin in particular) is disputed, so the antibody-to-injury link is curated as the prevailing model, not a settled fact. Retained deliberately alongside the supporting items so the dispute is visible on the edge.

treatments/0.description: First-line systemic immunosuppression with oral prednisone, often followed by or combined with conventional steroid-sparing agents (mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, cyclosporine, or methotrexate). Meta-analysis of 12 studies demonstrates that systemic therapy significantly slows progressive visual acuity loss, visual field loss, and cystoid macular edema. Response is variable; some patients stabilize while others progress despite treatment. No randomized controlled trials exist and no universally accepted protocol has been established.

treatments/2.description: Local intravitreal injections of sustained-release corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone implant, triamcinolone) provide targeted retinal immunosuppression, reducing inflammatory damage to photoreceptors and bipolar cells. evidence.snippet: Heterozygous loss-of-function mutations cause familial (benign) hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH) in which the lifelong mild hypercalcemia is generally asymptomatic. Homozygous inactivating mutations give rise to neonatal severe hyperparathyroidism (NSHPT) with extreme hypercalcemia and marked skeletal changes. evidence.snippet: Five heterozygous missense mutations (Asn118Lys, Phe128Leu, Thr151Met, Glu191Lys, and Phe612Ser) were detected in the extracellular domain of the calcium-sensing-receptor gene and shown to cosegregate with the disease.

genes/0.notes: Most reported pathogenic variants are heterozygous missense changes, distributed across extracellular, transmembrane and intracellular domains. Deletions, a nonsense variant, parental mosaicism and a rare homozygous case have also been reported. Variant-specific expression and signaling effects matter; a five-person NPSP795 study did not establish a reliable relationship between cellular assays and clinical drug response. Loss-of-function CASR variants usually cause the opposite calcium phenotype and should not be interpreted as ADH1 merely because the gene matches.

Tetany resolved, calcium and phosphate balance improved, and active vitamin D and calcium were stopped while low-dose hydrochlorothiazide, magnesium and potassium continued. Urinary calcium improved in the reported follow-up, but persistent hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia and the uncontrolled design limit claims of complete correction or renal protection. treatments/4.description: Investigational negative allosteric modulators reduce CaSR signaling. A three-day NPSP795 study in five adults increased PTH without significant improvement in ionized calcium or fractional calcium excretion. An uncontrolled encaleret phase 2b study in 13 adults improved serum calcium and hypercalciuria over 24 outpatient weeks. The 2026 CALIBRATE conference report adds randomized phase 3 evidence: at week 24, 75.6% of encaleret participants achieved both blood and urine calcium targets, compared with 19% in the concurrent standard-care group. The primary comparison was separately within the encaleret arm against its own pretreatment standard-care period (75.6% versus 4.4%). These are biochemical endpoints reported in a conference abstract; long-term kidney protection is not established. FDA accepted the encaleret application in July 2026, with approval still pending at review. AXT914 and related quinazolinones have preclinical evidence, not established clinical ADH1 efficacy.

Baseline renal activation is allele- and calcium-dependent rather than obligatorily maximal in every patient. Raising serum calcium may recruit or worsen renal calcium losses, so symptom relief must be balanced against urine calcium and renal outcomes. This supports individualized targets, not withholding acute calcium treatment or assuming every patient has the same threshold.

open_questions/1.rationale: The five-adult NPSP795 study found no significant correlation between its cellular assay readouts and clinical PTH response. Small sample size, brief exposure and within-allele variability limit this negative result. Leu723Arg demonstrates G11-biased signaling in HEK293 cells, while other tested ADH1 variants activate multiple pathways. This establishes possible assay dependence but does not prove that signaling bias caused clinical nonresponse or short stature. Proposed residue contacts and genotype-guided drug selection require further validation.

open_questions/2.rationale: Low calcium with insufficient PTH occurs in ADH1, other genetic hypoparathyroidism and acquired parathyroid disorders. All may have renal treatment complications; urine calcium alone is not a definitive discriminator. Pathogenic activating CASR variants distinguish ADH1 from GNA11-related ADH2 and from other molecular causes. Activating CaSR autoantibodies are an acquired phenocopy, but a negative CASR test also warrants assessment of other genetic causes, surgery, autoimmunity and magnesium disturbances.

evidence.snippet: However, the NEK1 mutants which weakened association with C21ORF2 did not rescue C21ORF2 expression, consistent with the possibility that complex formation regulates C21ORF2 stability (Fig S7B).

steps/4.description: Endogenous CFAP410 associates tightly with NEK1 in ARPE-19 cells. The NEK1 C-terminal region spanning residues 1160-1286 is necessary and sufficient for association in cellular assays. AlphaFold predicts an interface with the CFAP410 N-terminal leucine-rich repeat region, supported by mutagenesis, but direct binding of purified proteins was not demonstrated. Tested disease-associated variants reduce association to different degrees. In NEK1-knockout cells, both wild-type and kinase-dead NEK1 restored CFAP410 abundance, whereas association-defective variants did not; kinase activity and complex-dependent abundance are therefore separable requirements.

evidence.snippet: Depletion of NEK1 and C21ORF2 resulted in a dramatic reduction in HR efficiency, similar in effect size to depletion of BRCA1.
evidence.explanation: Direct result from a cell-based homologous-recombination reporter assay; not a demonstration of DNA damage in patient tissues.

steps/5.description: Depletion of CFAP410 or NEK1 reduces homologous recombination in U2-O-S traffic-light and DR-GFP reporter assays. CFAP410 depletion had little effect on cell-cycle distribution, arguing against a cell-cycle explanation for its repair phenotype. Whether this repair defect contributes to skeletal dysplasia or retinal degeneration in axial SMD remains untested.

evidence.snippet: Biochemical approaches place C21orf2 within key ciliopathy-associated protein modules, offering an explanation for the skeletal and retinal involvement observed in individuals with C21orf2 variants.
evidence.explanation: An unbiased genome-wide screen, not a candidate-gene experiment, placing the protein in the ciliary machinery and connecting that to the two affected tissues.

evidence.snippet: Our study indicates that axial SMD is a member of a unique group of ciliopathy affecting skeleton and retina.
evidence.explanation: The classification of the disease as a ciliopathy by the group that identified its first gene.

evidence.snippet: As shown in Fig 5D and E, the proportion of NEK1–KO and C21ORF2–KO cells bearing primary cilia was reduced dramatically compared with parental cells.
evidence.explanation: Loss of either gene impairs primary ciliogenesis in ARPE-19 cells.

steps/6.description: NEK1 or CFAP410 knockout markedly reduces the proportion of ciliated ARPE-19 cells after serum starvation. Wild-type re-expression rescues ciliogenesis, whereas kinase-dead NEK1 and the association-defective NEK1 p.Asp1277Ala allele do not. These epithelial-cell experiments establish a ciliary function but do not directly assay an axial SMD growth plate or patient photoreceptor.

evidence.snippet: C21orf2 protein was localized to the connecting cilium of the cone and rod photoreceptors, confirming its significance in retinal function.
evidence.explanation: AAV reporter and fusion-protein localization in mouse retina supports the ciliary site of action; this was not a patient-cell dysfunction or treatment-rescue experiment.

steps/7.description: CFAP410 localizes to the connecting cilium and basal-body structures of photoreceptors. This supports a ciliary site of disease action, but patient photoreceptor transport failure was not measured in the cited studies. Reduced stability of selected variants was demonstrated separately in transfected HEK293T cells, not in patient photoreceptors.

evidence.snippet: Knock-down of C21orf2 caused significant decreases in expression of chondrocyte marker genes (Fig 5).
evidence.explanation: Perturbation in OUMS-27 cells supports altered maintenance of cartilage-marker expression, not a direct growth-plate histopathology finding.

evidence.snippet: While the expression of cartilage marker genes (Col2a1, Agc1 and Col10a1) was increased by the cartilage induction, 1810043G02Rik expression was continuously suppressed during cartilage differentiation (Fig 4).
evidence.explanation: The ATDC5 time course is an expression association, not a loss-of-function differentiation experiment.

steps/8.description: CFAP410 knockdown in OUMS-27 human chondrosarcoma cells reduces expression of chondrocyte marker genes, suggesting a role in maintaining the differentiated chondrocyte phenotype. In a separate mouse ATDC5 differentiation time course, Cfap410 transcript abundance decreased while cartilage markers increased. Neither experiment establishes failure of growth-plate differentiation in patients or identifies the intervening ciliary signal.

evidence.snippet: We show that NEK1 mutations that inhibit kinase activity or weaken its association with C21ORF2 severely compromise ciliogenesis, and that C21ORF2, like NEK1 is required for homologous recombination.

evidence.snippet: Taken together, we conclude that cells deficient in NEK1 or C21ORF2 have a major defect in HR.

genes/0.notes: Formerly C21orf2 or LRRC76; 21q22.3. The 2016 axial SMD study identified five distinct alleles (three missense and two splice-altering) in nine patients from six of nine families. The same gene causes a broader spectrum including isolated retinal dystrophy and Jeune-like skeletal ciliopathy. In the ophthalmically ascertained 2025 series, 11/49 patients had skeletal abnormalities, which were broader than a uniform axial SMD diagnosis; five patients lacked a documented skeletal examination. This is not penetrance of axial SMD among all biallelic carriers.

evidence.explanation: The CFAP410-negative families supported genetic heterogeneity in 2016, before NEK1 was identified; they do not prove that testing both currently known genes leaves these same cases unexplained.

genes/1.notes: A patient with axial SMD carried compound heterozygous NEK1 c.3107C>G (p.Ser1036Ter) and c.3830A>C (p.Asp1277Ala). NEK1 is a CFAP410-associated protein and also causes other skeletal ciliopathies. Both variants reduce CFAP410 association in cellular assays. The unresolved CFAP410-negative patients in the earlier 2016 study preceded discovery of NEK1 as the second locus and do not by themselves establish a third disease gene.

evidence.snippet: The main clinical findings are postnatal growth failure, rhizomelic short stature in early childhood evolving into short trunk in late childhood, and thoracic hypoplasia that may cause mild to moderate respiratory problems in the neonatal period and later susceptibility to airway infection.

evidence.snippet: A minority of patients (22.4%) presented with skeletal abnormalities consistent with axial spondylometaphyseal dysplasia (SMDAX).

treatments/2.description: Counseling should address autosomal recessive inheritance and variable skeletal involvement. treatments/3.description: Early chest expansion surgery corrected pectus excavatum and a narrow thorax in one patient with CFAP410-associated retinal and skeletal disease. This is a reported intervention, not evidence of a general surgical indication or comparative efficacy.

open_questions/0.rationale: The step from defective ciliogenesis to the skeletal lesion is the weakest link in this pathograph and the entry marks the edge INDIRECT_UNKNOWN_INTERMEDIATES for that reason. In other skeletal ciliopathies the mechanism is impaired Hedgehog transduction through failed ciliary translocation of GLI transcription factors, and that is a reasonable expectation here, but no Hedgehog readout, no GLI localization, and no growth-plate histology has been reported in an axial SMD patient or model. The only chondrocyte-level datum is a functional result described by its own authors as suggesting involvement in cartilage differentiation. Until a signalling readout is measured, the skeletal arm rests on analogy.

open_questions/1.rationale: The CFAP410-NEK1 complex has two demonstrated functions and this disease could in principle be caused by either. The repair arm is modelled here as a node with no downstream edge, which is deliberate: nothing published connects it to a tissue phenotype in axial SMD. The reason it is not simply omitted is that the same complex is implicated in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, where the DNA repair function is the favoured mechanism, so which arm matters may be tissue-dependent rather than settled.

open_questions/2.rationale: The distribution is characteristic but not absolute: the 2016 series also recorded metacarpal metaphyseal abnormalities and one patient with other long-bone involvement. Tissue-specific requirements and modifiers remain hypotheses.

open_questions/3.rationale: The 2023 mammalian knockout and 2025 algal knockout studies differ in organism, cilium type and assay conditions. The algal report also differs internally between numerical reductions in Results and a lack of significance in Discussion. Cell-cycle effects and compensation remain hypotheses.

evidence.snippet: CHIME syndrome is characterized by colobomas, heart defects, ichthyosiform dermatosis, mental retardation (intellectual disability), and ear anomalies, including conductive hearing loss. Whole-exome sequencing on five previously reported cases identified PIGL, the de-N-acetylase required for glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor formation, as a strong candidate.

steps/1.description: Mutations in PIGL gene disrupt glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor biosynthesis. PIGL encodes a de-N-acetylase required for GPI anchor formation, essential for anchoring various cell surface proteins including receptors, enzymes, and adhesion molecules.

evidence.snippet: Furthermore, cell lines derived from these cases had significantly reduced levels of the two GPI anchor markers, CD59 and a GPI-binding toxin, aerolysin (FLAER), confirming the pathogenicity of the mutations.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates functional consequences of PIGL mutations showing reduced GPI anchor markers in patient cells.

steps/2.description: Reduced levels of GPI-anchored proteins on cell surface due to impaired biosynthesis, affecting normal cellular functions and signaling pathways. This leads to the multisystem phenotype characteristic of CHIME syndrome.

evidence.snippet: CHIME syndrome is a rare autosomal recessive neuroectodermal disorder associated with biallelic mutations in PIGL. To date, six molecularly confirmed cases of CHIME syndrome have been reported. Here, we report the seventh patient with biallelic PIGL mutations associated with CHIME syndrome and describe the first characterization of an intragenic deletion in PIGL.

evidence.snippet: In CHIME syndrome, a recurrent missense mutation c.500T > C (p.Leu167Pro) is found in the majority of patients, associated with a null mutation in the other allele, including an overrepresentation of large deletions. The latter are not detected by the standard analysis in sequencing techniques, including next-generation sequencing. Thus, in individuals with a clinical diagnosis of CHIME syndrome in which only one mutation is found, an active search for a large deletion should be sought.
evidence.explanation: Ceroni et al. 2018 establishes that large deletions are a common mutational mechanism in CHIME syndrome, often missed by standard sequencing, and recommends active screening for deletions in diagnostic workup.

steps/3.description: Variants on both ADAMTS13 alleles abolish or severely reduce production of functional ADAMTS13 protein. ADAMTS13 is synthesised mainly in hepatic stellate cells and also in vascular endothelial cells, so the deficiency is a plasma-protein deficiency rather than a lesion in the target vessel wall. That distinction is what makes the disease correctable from outside: the microvasculature itself is normal.

evidence.snippet: An evaluation of overt disease onset in all patients with an available sensitive ADAMTS13 activity assay (n=97) shows that residual ADAMTS13 activity is not the only determinant of age at first disease manifestation.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the claim that residual activity does not fully determine phenotype, which is the basis for the knowledge gap recorded below.

steps/4.description: Circulating VWF-cleaving metalloprotease activity is at or below 10% of normal, with no functional inhibitor present. Residual activity varies between genotypes and, importantly, is not by itself sufficient to predict when disease will first manifest.

evidence.snippet: Cleavage of vWF appears to be modulated by shear force, binding to platelet or platelet glycoprotein-1balpha, heparin, inflammatory cytokine (interleukin-6), and chloride ion.

steps/5.description: Uncleaved ultralarge VWF multimers remain in plasma and anchored to endothelium. Their adhesive function is shear-dependent, and ADAMTS13 proteolysis of VWF is itself modulated by shear force and by binding to platelet glycoprotein Ib-alpha, so the substrate is most dangerous exactly where the enzyme is most needed.

evidence.snippet: Deficiency of plasma ADAMTS13 activity, due to either an inherited or an acquired etiology, may lead to a potentially lethal syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

steps/6.description: Platelets bind the exposed A1 domains of unfurled ultralarge VWF and aggregate, building platelet-VWF thrombi in arterioles and capillaries. The thrombi are platelet- and VWF-rich rather than fibrin-rich, which is why coagulation screens are typically normal in TTP.
